title: Maximum Number of Darts Inside of a Circular Dartboard
statement:
Several darts are stuck in a huge wall; `darts[i] = [x_i, y_i]` gives the position of dart `i`, and no two darts share a position. You may hang a circular dartboard of radius `r` anywhere on the wall (its center does not have to be at integer coordinates).

A dart counts as on the board when its distance from the board's center is at most `r`, so darts exactly on the rim count. Return the largest number of darts that one placement of the board can cover.
constraints: All darts are at distinct positions
notes:
## Intuition

Take any placement that covers the most darts. Slide the board until a covered dart touches the rim, then rotate it around that dart until a second covered dart touches the rim; nothing falls off along the way. So unless only one dart can be covered, some optimal board has **two darts on its rim**. Two points at distance at most `2r` lie on the rim of exactly two circles of radius `r` (one when the distance is exactly `2r`), so trying every pair and counting darts for each of its two centers finds the answer.

## Approach

1. Start `best` at 1: a board centered on any dart covers it.
2. For each pair `i < j`, compute the squared distance `distSq`. If it exceeds `(2r)²`, no board of radius `r` has both on its rim; skip.
3. Otherwise the centers sit on the perpendicular bisector, at distance `h = sqrt(r² - distSq / 4)` from the midpoint `(midX, midY)`, on either `side`.
4. For each center `(cx, cy)`, count the darts with distance at most `r + eps`; `eps` absorbs rounding error for darts that sit exactly on the rim.
5. Keep the largest `count` in `best` and return it.

## Example 1, step by step

`darts = [[-2,0],[2,0],[0,2],[0,-2]]`, `r = 2`. The pair `(-2,0)`, `(2,0)` has `distSq = 16 = (2r)²`, so `h = 0` and both sides give the center `(0, 0)`. Every dart is at distance exactly 2 from it, so `count = 4` and `best = 4`. No board can cover more than all four darts, so the answer is `4`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n³): O(n²) pairs, two centers each, and an O(n) count per center.
- Space: O(1) beyond the input.

## Pitfalls

- Darts on the rim count, and floating-point centers make their distances like `1.9999999999` or `2.0000000001`; compare with a small tolerance.
- Compare squared distances with integers for the `2r` test so the pair at exactly `2r` is not lost to rounding.
- Remember the answer is at least 1 even when no pair fits in a board.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `best` | most darts covered by any center tried so far |
| `i`, `j` | the two darts that will lie on the rim |
| `dx`, `dy`, `distSq`, `dist` | offset between the two darts, its squared length and length |
| `h` | distance from the pair's midpoint to each candidate center |
| `midX`, `midY` | midpoint of the two darts |
| `side` | which of the two centers (left or right of the pair) |
| `cx`, `cy` | the candidate center |
| `count` | darts covered by the board at `(cx, cy)` |
| `eps` | rounding tolerance for darts on the rim |

narration.3: A tiny tolerance so darts exactly on the rim still count despite rounding.
narration.4: A board centered on any one dart covers at least that dart.
narration.6: Pick the first dart that will lie on the board's rim.
narration.7: Pick a second dart, after the first, to lie on the rim too.
narration.12: Squared distance between the two darts, computed exactly in integers.
narration.13: Farther apart than the board's diameter: no board of radius r touches both.
narration.16: The real distance between the two darts.
narration.17: How far each center sits from the midpoint, along the perpendicular bisector (Pythagoras).
narration.20: Try the center on each side of the line through the two darts.
narration.21: Move from the midpoint by h along the unit perpendicular (-dy, dx) / dist.
narration.24: Look at every dart for this candidate board.
narration.25: Is the dart within r of the center, allowing for rounding?
narration.29: Keep the best count over all candidate boards.
narration.33: Some optimal board has two darts on its rim, so best is the answer.
